bywork: Work aside from regular work; subordinate or secondary business.
byview: A private or selfish view; self-interested aim or purpose. No by-views of his own shall mislead him. Atterbury.
byard: A piece of leather crossing the breast, used by the men who drag sledges in coal mines.
bywash: The outlet from a dam or reservoir; also, a cut to divert the flow of water.
byproduct: A secondary or additional product; something produced, as in the course of a manufacture, in addition to the principal product.
bystreet: A separate, private, or obscure street; an out of the way or cross street. He seeks by-streets, and saves the expensive coach. Gay.
bye: 1. A thing not directly aimed at; something which is a secondary object of regard; an object by the way, etc.; as in on or upon the bye, i.e., in passing; indirectly; by implication. [Obs. | 1. A dwelling. Gibson. 2. In certain games, a station or place of an individual player. Emerson.
byword: 1. A common saying; a proverb; a saying that has a general currency. I knew a wise man that had it for a byword. Bacon. 2. The object of a contemptuous saying. Thou makest us a byword among the heathen. Ps. xliv. 14
bystander: One who stands near; a spectator; one who has no concern with the business transacting. He addressed the bystanders and scattered pamphlets among them. Palfrey. Syn. -- Looker on; spectator; beholder; observer.
byblow: 1. A side or incidental blow; an accidental blow. With their by-blows they did split the very stones in pieces. Bunyan. 2. An illegitimate child; a bastard. The Aga speedily . . . brought her [his disgraced slave] to court, together with her pretty by-blow, the present Padre Ottomano. Evelyn.
bysmottered: Bespotted with mud or dirt. (old) Chaucer.
bywalk: secluded or private walk. He moves afterward in by-walks. Dryden.
byrespect: Private end or view; by-interest. (old) Dryden.
bygone: Past; gone by. "Bygone fooleries." Shak | Something gone by or past; a past event. "Let old bygones be" Tennyson. Let bygones be bygones, let the past be forgotten.
byname: To give a nickname to. Camden.
bystroke: An accidental or a slyly given stroke.
bypath: A private path; an obscure way; indirect means. God known, my son, By what bypaths, and indirect crooked ways, I met this crown. Shak.
byelection: An election held by itself, not at the time of a general election.
byzant: A gold coin, so called from being coined at Byzantium. See Bezant.
byend: Private end or interest; secret purpose; selfish advantage. [Written also bye-end.] "Profit or some other by-end." L'Estrange.
by: 1. In the neighborhood of; near or next to; not far from; close to; along with; as, come and sit by me. By foundation or by shady rivulet He sought them both. Milton. 2. On; along; in traversing. | 1. Near; in the neighborhood; present; as, there was no person by at the time. 2. Passing near; going past; past; beyond; as, the procession has gone by; a bird flew by. 3. Aside; as, to lay by;
byturning: An obscure road; a way turning from the main road. Sir P. Sidney.
bypass: A by-passage, for a pipe, or other channel, to divert circulation from the usual course.
byplay: Action carried on aside, and commonly in dumb show, while the main action proceeds.
byssolite: An olive-green fibrous variety of hornblende.
byssaceous: Byssuslike; consisting of fine fibers or threads, as some very delicate filamentous algæ.
bylaw: 1. A local or subordinate law; a private law or regulation made by a corporation for its own government. There was likewise a law to restrain the by-laws, or ordinances of corporations. Bacon. The law or institution; to which are added two by-laws, as a comment upon the general law. Addison. 2.
byway: A secluded, private, or obscure way; a path or road aside from the main one. " Take no byways." Herbert.
byre: A cow house. [N. of Eng.& Scot.]
bywipe: A secret or side stroke, as of raillery or sarcasm. Milton.
byspeech: An incidental or casual speech, not directly relating to the point. "To quote by-speeches." Hooker.
byzantine: A gold coin, so called from being coined at Byzantium. See Bezant. | Of or pertaining to Byzantium. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Byzantium, now Constantinople; sometimes, applied to an inhabitant of the modern city of Constantinople.
bybidder: One who bids at an auction in behalf of the auctioneer or owner, for the purpose of running up the price of articles. [U.S.]
bypassage: A passage different from the usual one; a byway.
bydependence: An appendage; that which depends on something else, or is distinct from the main dependence; an accessory. Shak.
byroom: A private room or apartment. "Stand in some by-room" Shak.
byroad: A private or obscure road. "Through slippery byroads" Swift.
byssine: Made of silk; having a silky or flaxlike appearance. Coles.
byronic: Pertaining to, or in the style of, Lord Byron. With despair and Byronic misanthropy. Thackeray
bylane: A private lane, or one opening out of the usual road.
byssus: 1. A cloth of exceedingly fine texture, used by the ancients. It is disputed whether it was of cotton, linen, or silk. [Written also byss and byssin.] 2. (Zoöl.) A tuft of long, tough filaments which are formed in a groove of the foot, and issue from between the valves of certain bivalve mollusks, as the Pinna and Mytilus, by which they attach themselves to rocks, etc. 3.
bycorner: A private corner. Britain being a by-corner, out of the road of the world. Fuller.
